sum: Palantir shares climbed 4.5% as a broad rebound in AI-related equities brought an eight-session losing streak to a halt, with investors returning to technology names after the recent selloff. Media reports put the gain in the context of a sector-wide recovery following a sharp drawdown earlier in the week. For anyone holding the stock, though, the bounce only sharpens the real question: can business momentum and a fresh batch of partnerships carry the recovery further?
The answer hinges less on sentiment than on execution. New agreements give the expansion concrete footholds, but their worth to the business will only emerge through successful rollout.

At the center of that test is how effectively Palantir moves the announced applications into its partners' day-to-day operations. On Thursday, Changshin unveiled a partnership to deploy Foundry and AIP across shoe development and manufacturing processes — a tangible new field of use for the two platforms, and one that spans both design and production.

The AmeriLife tie-up, announced the same day, adds useful context. Foundry and AIP are to be used in health and wealth distribution, and at Crump Life Insurance Services comparable applications were already running in live production. That detail matters to investors precisely because it goes beyond a bare announcement of cooperation.

Progress on such projects therefore serves as the yardstick. A lasting recovery would be supported if the announced usage broadens and shows up in revenue. The more clearly a partnership demonstrates economic weight, the more it reinforces that case.

The earnings release supplies a solid starting point for the bullish reading. Palantir reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year over year, and lifted its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to 91%. For the US commercial business, the company guided to 143% growth. Both figures are company expectations, and they set correspondingly demanding benchmarks for what comes next.
What counts is the link between growth already achieved and the additional room to deploy. The partnerships could support expansion — provided the planned applications turn into durable business.

sum: Palantir Technologies reported a sharp acceleration in its third-quarter business on November 2, 2026, with revenue growth reaching a company-record pace and its U.S. commercial operation overtaking government revenue for the first time. The results and outlook were published in a Business Wire release carried by Morningstar for the quarter ended September 30.

Revenue rose 96 percent year over year to 2.313 billion US dollars, passing the 2 billion dollar mark for the first time. Revenue also increased 20 percent from the previous quarter. U.S. revenue climbed 119 percent year over year to 1.937 billion dollars, with commercial revenue up 148 percent to 984 million dollars. U.S. government revenue rose 96 percent to 953 million dollars, leaving commercial sales ahead by 31 million dollars.

The shift in mix is central to the investment case. Palantir said its commercial business benefited from demand for its artificial intelligence platforms, including its Sovereign AI offering. Total commercial revenue increased 113 percent to 1.168 billion dollars, while the company closed 212 deals worth at least 1 million dollars. Total contract value reached 2.918 billion dollars, up 6 percent year over year, and U.S. commercial remaining deal value rose 79 percent to 6.517 billion dollars.

Profitability remained high, although the company reports both GAAP and adjusted measures. GAAP operating income reached 1.085 billion dollars, equal to a 47 percent margin, while adjusted operating income was 1.427 billion dollars, or a 62 percent margin. GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders was 1.128 billion dollars, and diluted GAAP earnings per share came to 0.44 dollar. Adjusted free cash flow was 1.216 billion dollars, representing a 53 percent margin.

Management raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to between 8.530 billion and 8.534 billion dollars. The midpoint implies 91 percent year-over-year growth. The U.S. commercial revenue outlook was lifted to more than 3.559 billion dollars, implying growth of at least 143 percent. Palantir also expects adjusted operating income of 5.245 billion to 5.249 billion dollars and adjusted free cash flow of 4.8 billion to 5.0 billion dollars for the year.

sum: Investing.com -- Palantir Technologies raised its full-year revenue forecast on Monday after reporting a 96% jump in third-quarter revenue, driven by accelerating demand for its artificial intelligence software in the United States, where commercial sales surpassed government revenue for the first time.

The software company reported revenue of $2.31 billion for the quarter ended September 30, compared with $1.18 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 20% sequentially, while U.S. revenue surged 119% year-over-year to $1.94 billion.

The results underscore the growing contribution of commercial customers to Palantir's business as companies accelerate investments in artificial intelligence and adopt its software to integrate AI models into operational workflows. It has rapidly incorporated the new technology into its business model, leading to skyrocketing revenue and earnings.

That said, Palantir's stock rally has slowed over the last 12 months, leaving investors wondering whether it can return to the explosive growth it enjoyed in previous years. Let's dig into the pros and cons of the stock to decide what it might be worth by the end of 2027.

Right now, AI-hungry investors are mostly limited to the infrastructure side of the opportunity. However, many leading consumer-facing AI software leaders are still privately held, putting them out of reach.

Palantir convincingly bucks the trend. Its business involves sifting through vast amounts of its clients' internal data to help them identify actionable insights like business trends, opportunities, and fraud. Generative AI proved highly synergistic with these tools, enabling operators to access insights via natural language prompts rather than advanced interfaces. Demand has been explosive.

Second-quarter revenue soared 93% year over year to $1.94 billion amid a surge of interest from U.S. commercial clients (which jumped 149%). American companies have shown a strong willingness to incorporate AI-related software into their operations. And Palantir is holding its own against industry rivals like Microsoft and Snowflake, which offer competing data analytics businesses.
Part of Palantir's economic moat may stem from a reputation for security, born of its extensive work with high-profile government clients such as the CIA, NATO, and the Department of Defense.

sum: As of Friday’s close, Palantir (PLTR) traded at about $176, roughly flat from a year ago. Yet over the past 12 months, the AI data analytics company’s revenue nearly doubled, quarterly operating income more than tripled, and its 2026 guidance was raised twice. The stock’s going nowhere isn’t because the market ignored its growth — it’s because that growth was absorbed into working down what was once an extremely stretched valuation.

Earnings data shows Palantir’s second-quarter revenue rose 93% year over year to about $1.94 billion, with U.S. commercial revenue growing 149% to $764 million. Profits expanded in tandem: operating income rose from $269 million to $912 million, lifting the operating margin from 27% to 47%; earnings per share rose from $0.13 to $0.41, more than tripling. More notably, the growth rate keeps climbing — revenue grew 48% in the same quarter last year, 85% in Q1 of this year, and 93% in Q2, a new high. CEO Alex Karp said in the earnings release: “This quarter was otherworldly.”

The pace of guidance raises is equally striking. Palantir opened 2026 guiding toward about $7.2 billion in revenue, raised that to about $7.65 billion in May, and again to about $8.15 billion in early August. A year ago at this point, management’s full-year 2025 revenue target was just about $4.15 billion. In one year, the company’s annual revenue target nearly doubled.

Yet the market cap has not swelled in step with the business. Palantir’s market capitalization sits at about $420 billion, little changed from a year ago. A year ago, that price amounted to about 100 times the 2025 revenue target; today, against this year’s $8.15 billion goal, it works out to about 52 times. The price is unchanged while the business has doubled in size, so the sales multiple has been halved. In other words, the market didn’t ignore Palantir’s growth — it absorbed it into the valuation, with each strong quarter and each guidance raise going toward working down the multiple rather than pushing the share price higher.
But even with the sales multiple halved, 52 times is still an extremely high premium. Measured against analysts’ expected earnings for next year, the forward price-to-earnings ratio is about 76.

sum: Palantir Technologies has named Nebius Group its preferred infrastructure partner for sovereign artificial intelligence, but the September 8 announcement left out the number that would turn the alliance into a financial event for Nebius: neither company disclosed a contract value, a customer commitment nor an expected revenue contribution.

Under the companies’ description of the partnership, Nebius compute and inference endpoints will become accessible inside Palantir’s enterprise environment after an integration period. Eligible commercial customers will be able to run open models on Nebius infrastructure while retaining control over their data, compute and models.

The arrangement also calls for the companies to bring new capacity online, including modular data centers at sites where power is already available. For Nebius, the practical attraction is distribution: Palantir already sells software into organizations with demanding security and data-governance requirements. A working integration could shorten the path between a customer’s AI application and the infrastructure needed to run it.

Yet “preferred” is not the same as purchased. The release does not describe the partnership as exclusive, identify a launch customer or specify a minimum amount of compute that Palantir will direct to Nebius. It also makes access contingent on an integration period and limits the initial opportunity to eligible Palantir customers. Those omissions do not negate the commercial value; they prevent investors from counting it as backlog.

Nebius is no longer starting from a small revenue base. Its second-quarter filing reported group revenue of $582.3 million, up 454% from a year earlier. sum: This is a hypergrowth chapter for Palantir, defined by U.S. demand the company cannot fully meet. Its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) serves foundational government clients like the Department of the Navy and commercial giants like GE Aerospace.

This intense demand has become the company’s biggest operational problem. To manage the pressure, leadership has surged resources from its commercial teams to support the acute needs of the defense industrial base.

Is the market pricing in that story reasonably at 138.0x trailing earnings? One clean way to test it is to compute the revenue growth implied by PLTR‘s current multiple and see whether the number lines up with how the business actually runs. Before we can get to that number, though, a few assumptions have to be locked in.
For PLTR’s stock price to make sense, three things have to play out. These are not predictions. They are what today’s price is implicitly requiring:

- Condition 1. The market gives the business 7 years to grow into the multiple. A multiple of 4.8x above mature levels needs years to grow into. A shorter window makes the math steeper; a longer one softens it.

- Condition 2. The multiple itself eventually settles at 28.8x, the multiple a mature, scaled software franchise typically settles into, blended with the company’s 3-year average, capped at 30x since its trailing history sits well above mature levels. A higher endpoint means today’s price needs less growth; a lower one needs more.

sum: Shares of data analytics company Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) fell 7% in the afternoon session after a confluence of high-profile AI talent departures from Alphabet, and a regulatory overhang pulled the entire communication-services and software complex lower.

Alphabet fell roughly 6%. Microsoft slipped as well. When the two largest software-adjacent megacaps decline together, the sector indices follow mechanically given their index weight.But the deeper driver was the market's persistent fear that AI agents would erode the subscription model that underpins traditional enterprise software economics. That fear had been compounding all year. Salesforce trades around $152, down roughly 43% year-to-date and near its 52-week low. Adobe fell approximately 49% over the past year and has not traded this cheap on earnings in over a decade.

The previous week's Accenture collapse, a near-20% single-day drop after the consulting giant cut its growth outlook and explicitly cited AI compressing demand for traditional IT services acted as a fresh confirmation of the thesis. If the largest IT services firm in the world is signaling that AI is eating its billable hours, investors extend the same logic to the software vendors whose products those hours configure.

The counterargument is that the selling has become indiscriminate. Salesforce is a Rule-of-40 company retiring 10% of its shares through a $25 billion buyback, carrying the largest AI revenue line in the category, and it is acquiring usage-based billing platforms like m3ter precisely to monetize AI agent actions rather than seats. Monness upgraded the stock to Buy the previous week on valuation. The market is pricing the cannibalization as if it already happened; the income statements might be indicating otherwise. But until these companies can prove that AI revenue scales faster than it erodes the legacy subscription base, software might remain in the penalty box even on days when the rest of tech (especially chip stocks) is celebrating.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) just posted the fastest growth in its history, and the stock has fallen apart anyway. Shares closed at $127.99 on June 12, leaving them 38% below the $207.52 high from last November. That drawdown of 38.22% is the deepest the stock has sat underwater in a year.

The disconnect is the story. Companies do not usually grow 85% and lose a third of their value at once. Bears say cheaper, smarter AI models will commoditize enterprise software and strip Palantir’s premium price. CEO Alex Karp says that fear is exactly why his customers keep coming back. The gap between $127.99 and the company’s own results is where the answer lives.

The bear case is not lazy. Even after the fall, Palantir trades at extreme multiples: an NTM P/E near 81x and an NTM EV/EBITDA around 58x, against a software peer median near 12x. That leaves no room for error.

The error now has a name. On June 9, Reuters reported that the UK is reviewing its £330 million NHS data contract and weighing a break clause in early 2027. London’s mayor had already blocked a separate £50 million police deal a month earlier. Suddenly, the international government business, about $172 million last quarter, looks like a political target. The stock dropped on the news because the most expensive software name falls hardest when sentiment turns.
Here is the turn. The thing bears fear, AI getting cheaper, is the thing management says fuels the business.

On June 10, Karp told CNBC that enterprises are frustrated with the frontier labs and accused them of “tokenmaxxing,” optimizing for how many AI tokens a customer burns rather than the result. That restates the Q1 call. CTO Shyam Sankar framed it as Jevons paradox, the rule that when something gets cheaper, you use far more of it. “Tokens are the new coal, AIP is the train,” he said. Cheaper models mean more tasks handed to AI, and more tasks without control means more errors.

sum: The numbers were, by any measure, extraordinary. But the debate they have ignited is anything but settled.

Palantir Technologies delivered second-quarter results that blew past Wall Street's expectations, sending shares surging nearly 30 percent in a single session and inflicting roughly $3 billion in mark-to-market losses on short sellers, according to data from S3 Partners. The move marked the stock's biggest one-day gain since early 2024 — and it has left both camps in the Palantir bull-bear battle feeling vindicated.

At the heart of the story is a company that appears to be operating at escape velocity. Revenue for the quarter jumped 93 percent year over year to $1.94 billion, with the US commercial segment — the crown jewel of the business — growing an eye-popping 149 percent to $764 million. GAAP net income more than tripled to $1.06 billion, or $0.41 per diluted share, while the adjusted operating margin hit a company-record 62 percent.

CEO Alex Karp described the performance as "beyond all expectations," and the company's guidance suggests management sees little reason to tap the brakes. Palantir now expects full-year 2026 revenue of $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion, up from its prior range of $7.65 billion to $7.66 billion — an implied annual growth rate of 82 percent. For the third quarter, the company guided to revenue between $2.160 billion and $2.164 billion, ahead of analyst consensus.

Operationally, the quarter showcased how broad demand has become. Palantir closed 220 contracts worth more than $1 million each, including 70 deals exceeding $10 million. Total contract value climbed 49 percent to $3.37 billion. The company also highlighted its "Apollo x NVIDIA" collaboration, in which automated agents handle model testing and architecture adjustments, and pointed to a new partnership with Google Cloud that will integrate Palantir's platform with BigQuery and Gemini. Law firm Kirkland & Ellis has meanwhile adopted Palantir's AIP platform to make internal knowledge more accessible.

Karp has set an ambitious target: within 18 months, he wants the entire global business to match the growth pace of the US commercial segment. That is a high-stakes bet that presupposes the current AI cycle has plenty of runway left.

sum: Few companies are doing as well as Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR). It just announced another impressive quarter, with revenue growth coming in at an outstanding 85% year over year. With a growth rate like that, it may seem like the sky is the limit for Palantir, but growth isn't everything with a stock. There are several considerations investors must account for when examining a stock, and growth is only one of them.
Along with strong growth, Palantir is also highly profitable

Palantir's growth rate is admittedly impressive. Its commercial segment more than doubled year over year, with revenue rising 104%. Palantir maintains a dual-sided business, with nearly half of its revenue from government clients and the other half from commercial. Both of these client bases are important, and the strength of each showcases the flexibility and performance of Palantir's AI-powered data analytics software.

But revenue isn't everything; if Palantir is operating at a loss to push its product into the hands of more users, this growth rate becomes less impressive. However, Palantir is also extremely profitable. In the first quarter, its GAAP profit margin was an impressive 53%. That's among the best profit margins I've ever seen from a software company, further underscoring that Palantir is one of the highest-performing software companies.

But what about Palantir's valuation? With all this success, a high valuation has come, and it's my one gripe against the stock. The best investments bought at the wrong price can still be bad investments, and Palantir is right on the borderline. Currently, Palantir trades for about 93 times forward earnings and 154 times trailing earnings.

So, even after Wall Street analysts project a very strong year for Palantir, its stock will still be pricey. There aren't many examples of profitable companies growing as quickly as Palantir is, so the best comparison I can point to is Nvidia.

During its latest quarter, Nvidia's growth rate was 73%, and it trades for 45 times trailing earnings and 26 times forward earnings. Palantir's profits would need to triple to trade in the same range as Nvidia, indicating several more years of strong growth are already priced into the stock.

sum: WASHINGTON — As recently as last year, Rep. Julie Johnson bought and sold stocks from Palantir Technologies, a contractor with the federal government that has been key to the Trump administration’s efforts to track and deport undocumented immigrants.

Johnson, a Farmers Branch Democrat who was elected in 2024 to represent Texas’ 32rd Congressional District, bought Palantir stock days before President Donald Trump took office for his second term on Jan. 15, 2025, and again on Feb. 12, 2025, according to congressional financial disclosure reports. In her role as vice ranking member, she urged Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to follow the Constitution in the department’s deportation efforts in May, demanding transparency about the Dallas Police Department’s cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in August and pressed Noem again in December about ICE’s conduct in Dallas.

The software specialist, which initially made its name by selling software and analytics solutions to U.S. intelligence agencies and the military, is now experiencing a remarkable upturn in its fortunes, thanks to the booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) software.

An investment of $10,000 in shares of Palantir five years ago would now be worth just over $93,000, with an average annual return rate of 56.4%. However, the stock has experienced its share of volatility during that time, enduring a period of slowing growth in 2022 and 2023 before stepping on the gas once again in 2024.

The good part is that Palantir's AI-driven growth continues to accelerate. However, will the drivers of the business be sufficient to enable the stock to replicate its remarkable performance over the next five years?

In 2020, Palantir's revenue rose 47% to $1.1 billion. For 2025, its revenue forecast stands at almost $4.4 billion, which would be a jump of nearly 54% over last year. So, Palantir's revenue has grown by almost four times in just five years, for a compound annual growth rate of almost 32%.

However, as the company's 2025 revenue guidance indicates, it is now growing at a significantly faster pace than previously. That's a result of the fast-growing adoption of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which it launched in April 2023. This platform has turned out to be a major success for the company, as it allows customers to integrate generative AI into their operations.

Palantir customers can utilize AIP for building, customizing, and managing AI applications tailored to their specific business needs. The good part is that its customers are witnessing improvements in productivity, reductions in redundancy, and higher efficiency by integrating generative AI. As a result, customers who initially adopt AIP usually go on to deploy this platform to more areas of their operations. This enterprise-wide adoption of AIP is helping Palantir score bigger and longer contracts.
So, it was not surprising to see Palantir land $2.8 billion worth of contracts in the third quarter, a jump of 151% from the prior-year quarter.

Denver-based Palantir is a data mining company that uses its powerful Gotham and Foundry platforms to help customers sort data and provide real-time analytics. Both Gotham and Foundry are incorporated into Palantir's groundbreaking Artificial Intelligence Platform, which uses interactive chat-style AI to allow users to access the platforms with minimal training.

The company has its roots as a government contractor that works with the military and intelligence agencies and famously was credited with helping to pinpoint the location of 9/11 mastermind Osama bin Laden. AIP has allowed Palantir to expand to other branches of government, as well as commercial businesses, as it helps manage supply chains, inventories, and provides predictive analysis so management can best position their companies for success.

PLTR has been one of the hottest stocks in the stock market for the last two years, up 145% so far this year. It now sports a market capitalization of about $453 billion. Earnings in the third quarter showed gains of 63% on a year-over-year (YoY) basis to $1.18 billion. U.S. commercial revenue was up 121% to $397 million. U.S. government revenue was $486 million, increasing 52% from a year ago.

If You'd Invested $100 in Palantir Technologies Stock 5 Years Ago, Here's How Much You'd Have Today
sum: Artificial intelligence leader Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) had a rough time after Michael Burry, the famous investor known for successfully shorting stocks, disclosed a bet against the stock recently. That sent the shares of Palantir down almost 10%.

But that doesn't change the fact that Palantir has been one of the best-performing stocks in the S&P 500 index over the past few years. And, in fact, it was the top performer in that index of large-cap companies last year, with a 340.5% return.

And over the past five years, Palantir's return has been an astounding 1,695% through market close Nov. 4. Needless to say, that return absolutely crushed the S&P 500's, which climbed about 97% in those five years.

So, if you had invested $100 in Palantir five years ago on Nov. 4, 2020, when the stock traded at about $16 a share, today your shares would be worth around $1,750. It's not a fortune, but remember that your initial investment was modest.

That return is due purely to capital appreciation, as Palantir doesn't pay dividends. And it probably shouldn't. Instead, the company chooses to expand the business, as it stated in a 2020 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. That strategy has paid off for Palantir shareholders in a big way over the past five years.

items.t: Short selling AI shares, Palantir boss calls Michael Burry 'crazy'
sum: JAKARTA – Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp has once again launched a sharp critique of short sellers, this time taking direct aim at legendary investor Michael Burry, known for his portrayal in the film The Big Short.
“The two companies he’s shorting are the ones making all the money, it’s very strange,” Karp told CNBC’s Squawk Box on Tuesday (4 November).
“The idea that chips and Ontology are what you want to short is completely mad,” he continued. “He’s essentially shorting AI—his targets are us and Nvidia.”

In a recent regulatory filing, Burry’s investment firm Scion Asset Management was revealed to hold large short positions in the two tech giants—put options on 5 million Palantir shares worth around US$912 million, and 1 million Nvidia shares valued at approximately US$187 million as of 30 September. Put options typically profit when share prices fall.
Karp accused Burry of “market manipulation” and targeting the wrong companies amid the current wave of investment enthusiasm in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

“With these short sellers, it’s all very complex—to be honest, I think it’s a form of market manipulation,” he said. “We’ve delivered the best results ever. It’s not even clear whether he’s doing this just to exit his position.”

Burry, who gained fame for predicting the US housing crisis ahead of the 2008 financial crash, declined to comment when contacted by CNBC. However, in a post on platform X (formerly Twitter) last week, he hinted at a potential market bubble.
